A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RLHF and trustworthiness study by the same authors. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial revisions.

before.justification: v1 reports original Pythia experiments across five trustworthiness tasks, plus toxicity-probe and output-distribution analyses in Appendix B.

after.justification: v2 reports original Pythia and Llama-7B evaluations, training-data toxicity measurements, format-adherence results and data-attribution analyses.

M1.justification: v2 introduces an RLHF-specific DataInf attribution procedure absent from v1: stage-specific losses, reward-model attribution for PPO, paired evaluation responses and normalized contribution scores. Appendix H adds conversion of fully fine-tuned weights to rank-4 LoRA approximations using SVD. This is a substantial new analytical method alongside the retained alignment algorithms.

E1.justification: Both versions retain Anthropic HH training data and the same five evaluation tasks: RealToxicityPrompts, demographic stereotype statements, ETHICS commonsense judgments, TruthfulQA and synthetic privacy leakage. Benign/adversarial prompt scenarios are retained. The added analyses examine existing data; model selection and scoring changes concern experimental settings.

E2.justification: Corresponding benchmark comparisons retain the unaligned baseline, SFT, PPO and DPO. Baseline and No-RLHF identify the same comparator. The new attribution section discusses alternative attribution approaches but does not experimentally compare them.

E3.justification: v2 removes Pythia-70M/160M/410M, adds Pythia-1.4B and Llama-7B, and retains 2.8B/6.9B. Bias and ethics switch from Yes/No token-probability comparisons to parsed generated responses. Truthfulness changes from three sampled outputs at temperature 0.5 with five beams to one nonsampled output at temperature 0.01 with three beams (v1 Table C1; v2 Table D1). The output-distribution analysis also changes metric and prompt aggregation.

E4.justification: v2 adds chosen-versus-rejected training-response toxicity analysis, output-format checks, attribution case studies and contribution-score distributions. It removes v1's toxicity-probe analysis and alternative-toxicity-metric checks. The output-distribution investigation is retained but revised from mean log-probabilities across four prompt settings to reported perplexities for toxic prompts with benign instructions. Existing adversarial-prompt checks remain.

E5.justification: v1 presents point estimates without uncertainty bars. v2 reports standard-deviation bars from five independent runs throughout the benchmark evaluation, plus standard deviations from five generations per prompt in Table G1. Five per-prompt toxicity generations were already documented in v1; the new reporting does not establish a specific increase in training repetitions.

E6.justification: Under revised settings, v2 replaces v1's findings of DPO harming ethics and improving privacy with ethics improvements and increased privacy leakage (v1 Tables 3-5; v2 Figures 3-4). v2 reports average ethics FNR of 56.8% before alignment versus 38.3% after PPO and 40.3% after DPO. Toxicity findings become negligible or uncertain overall. Attribution, format-adherence and training-response toxicity results are added, while probe and alternative-toxicity results disappear. These are revised findings, not same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: Section 5 adds influence-function mathematics, its DataInf approximation, stage-specific attribution losses and a normalized contribution-score definition (Equations 8-13). It introduces convexity and influence-stability reasoning without proving the convexity assertion. Separately, v2's DPO objective restores SFT-reference probability ratios absent from v1's formula, and the earlier DPO gradient expression is removed.

C1.justification: The overarching claim that RLHF does not guarantee trustworthiness remains. However, v2's introduction and conclusion replace the earlier algorithm-specific tradeoffs with negligible toxicity effects and ethics as the only consistently improved benchmark. They also elevate RLHF data attribution and identification of detrimental training examples to a principal contribution and introduce a first-systematic-evaluation novelty claim.

C2.justification: v1 explains increased toxicity through stronger toxic representations and narrower SFT/PPO output distributions. v2 emphasizes residual toxicity in chosen responses, pairwise preference effects and data-attribution explanations; Appendix G now includes DPO in distribution narrowing. v2 also expects similar trends in larger models, replacing v1's more preliminary generalization framing, while adding qualifications that attribution is post hoc and assumes influential examples remain important through training.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies the approximately 100,000-example static HH subset, full-parameter tuning, shared SFT initialization and GPT-j-6B reward model. Appendix C supplies algorithm/model-specific training hyperparameters, trlX and four A100 80GB GPUs; Appendix H documents attribution implementation. These substantially expand v1's sparse training documentation without establishing that every disclosed setting changed. The code link also changes repository owner and path.

R1.justification: The new Related Work section substantially expands positioning around conflicting alignment goals and efficient attribution. It introduces influence-function and DataInf references, discusses retraining and checkpoint-based attribution alternatives, and distinguishes the study from prior agent-development work. This establishes a new attribution-focused research contribution beyond v1's distributed background citations.

P1.justification: The title is shortened, and the abstract, introduction, contribution framing and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Preliminaries become a consolidated background section after Related Work, explanatory discussion becomes a substantial separate section, and the standalone limitations section disappears. Existing appendix material is reorganized alongside dedicated configuration and analysis sections.

P2.justification: Most line plots and accompanying numerical benchmark tables are replaced by grouped bar charts with error bars. Adversarial bias/ethics plots move to Appendix F, and the summary table becomes part of Figure 4. v2 adds a workflow diagram, attribution radar charts, scored examples, a histogram and training-configuration tables. Prompt examples are also compressed and repaginated.

improvement.justification: v2 improves reproducibility and empirical interpretation through explicit training configurations, uncertainty reporting, format-adherence checks and evaluation on a second model family, addressing important omissions in v1. The net gain is limited by the loss of exact benchmark tables and weaknesses in the new central attribution contribution: Section 5's convexity justification is unsubstantiated, and validation relies mainly on score patterns and selected examples rather than retraining or pruning experiments.
